en: The General Principles of the *Mahābrahmādeva-rāja-prcchā-buddha-vinodana-saṃdeha-sūtra*:
This entire scroll consists of twenty-four chapters, the titles of which are listed below. The scroll has now been produced in two volumes.
This sutra has remained hidden within the scripture cases of a certain temple for three hundred years;
consequently, many of its characters have been eaten away by bookworms, which we have filled with circles. There are also instances where pages have become detached, which is truly lamentable.
As for the origins of this sutra, I do not dare speak of them clearly; it is because it has been entrusted to me as a secret treasury that I strictly admonish against disclosing its provenance.
May those who read it refrain from engaging in forced interpretations.
This sutra was kept secret within the Imperial Archives in China and was not permitted to circulate; therefore, those who have seen it are exceedingly rare.

That this manuscript fortunately exists in our own country is truly a treasure of the state. We rely solely upon those with the power to propagate it, for we truly know that the words of Lord Wang Jinggong and Song Jinglian were not in vain.
This scripture was transcribed through successive copying, and the name of its translator has been lost; do not find this strange.
This single chapter, "Requesting Further Explanation," shares the same textual structure, phrasing, and meaning as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;

it differs only in that various passages in the middle have had characters added. However, the characters are most severely eroded; therefore, I have restored the full text according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Thus, the principle becomes manifest.
This scripture was separately requested by Brahmā-rāja during the assembly at the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, whereupon the Tathāgata expounded it once more for him;
therefore, its textual structure and phrasing are largely identical to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, with only minor differences.
I have kept this sutra deeply secret for fifty years now. Having encountered the sagely and enlightened [ruler], it is now being widely disseminated.

I humbly consider this to be a magnificent era of five hundred years. Having seen and heard of the various masters, I prostrate and hope that you will rejoice in its circulation and spread it far and wide.

The beginning and end of this sutra were separately and definitively categorized as "sudden" (dun) by the two masters Tiantai and Xuanzang. If one reads it with a sincere mind until it is thoroughly mastered, then the essential meaning of the sutra will be understood with complete precision and no omissions.
It is said that our country’s Great Master Cijue of Mount Tiantai once personally transcribed this sutra from the Great Tang and brought it back here.
In such-and-such a country, at such-and-such a monastery, I intended to personally collate and correct [this text]. However, being old, I am unable to do so; I shall await future worthies for a time.
Thus, Wuzhuo respectfully records this preface to the *Catalogue of the Sūtra on the Questions of Mahābrahmādeva and the Resolution of Doubts Concerning the Buddha*.

*The Sutra on the Great Brahma King Asking the Buddha to Resolve His Doubts*, Volume One.
The First Assembly: Chapter One on the Entrustment of the Dharma.

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one hundred billion bhikṣus, Śakra Devendra, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the Sovereign Son of Heaven (Īśvara), and Brahmā, Lord of the World.
O King, Śikhin, Mahā... Mahā-nāga-rāja, Kiṃnara, ... Asura, Garuḍa, ...
tree deities, palace deities, hearth deities, fire deities, wind deities, water deities, earth deities, and celestial deities.
The spirits of empty space; all malevolent spirits; all wandering spirits; wild ghosts and spirits; spirits of nightmares, curses, and pestilence;
the Sun and Moon Devas; the Stellar Devas; and the Devas of the Six Heavens of Desire and the Form Realm.
The devas of the four empty abodes, the Śuddhāvāsa devas of the Thirty-three Heavens, and all classes of sentient beings gathered together;
those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals of various different species; the sixteen great kings, immeasurable minor kings, and the various wheel-turning sage-kings;
and the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of this land and other lands—all surrounded him in silence.
[He] sat down cross-legged. The radiance from his *uṣṇīṣa* shone universally upon all Buddha-fields. The light of the various Buddhas came and entered the Buddha’s mouth.
The great assembly, seeing this auspicious omen, regarded it as rare and marvelous. They then bowed their heads and gazed [upon him].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying: "Today my back aches; the day of my *nirvāṇa* is near."
Immediately rising from his seat and lifting his feet, he proceeded toward the great city of Kuśinagara.

An immeasurable multitude, immeasurable beings of various kinds, immeasurable bodhisattvas, immeasurable devas, immeasurable wheel-turning sage kings (*cakravartin*), and others, all equally struck with alarm and longing, surrounded him from front and back.
Upon reaching the place where the Buddha was, they all sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One looked in the four directions and said: "The time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived today.
If you have any doubts, you may each ask about them one by one; do not delay."
Then the Great Brahmā King immediately led his numerous retinue to come forth, presenting *uḍumbara* flowers to the World-Honored One;
each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One took up a *pāṭala* flower offered to him, blinked his eyes, and raised his eyebrows to show it to the great assembly.
At that moment, the great assembly remained silent and speechless. Then, Kāśyapa broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said, "I possess the treasury of the true Dharma-eye and the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*; I now entrust this to you. You are able..."
[To] protect and maintain [it], continuing it without interruption. At that time, Kāśyapa, having received the Buddha’s command, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew.
Chapter Two: The Great Brahmā King Resolving Doubts.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King rose, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how most rare! World-Honored One.”
"How most rare! For fifty years, such a thing as this has never occurred; nor have we ever harbored such doubts regarding the World-Honored One.
Those present in this assembly are likewise so. We pray that you will resolve these doubts for us and for the multitude in this assembly, as well as for those who seek the Dharma in the future age.
We beseech you with earnest devotion to dispel our ignorance and delusion."
The World-Honored One previously taught the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and bestowed predictions of Buddhahood upon them all; could there possibly be any remaining?

The World-Honored One is fully endowed with the three mysteries, possesses the four types of eloquence and the eight qualities of voice, and his perfect and complete preaching leaves nothing unexhausted; yet there is nothing heard that is not realized.
Nevertheless, the World-Honored One now plucks a flower and shows it to the assembly, at which point the World-Honored One immediately has words of entrustment. The World-Honored One—
“I and those present in this assembly do not understand its meaning and intent. We only pray that you will resolve these doubts in our minds.
At that time, the Buddha said, “Excellent, Brahmā King! It is well that you have asked such a question for the sake of those in this assembly and for the sake of future generations.”
"How extraordinary! Listen attentively, listen attentively. For your sake, I shall now provide a definitive resolution so that you may understand and have no further doubts;
[you shall] swiftly [attain realization]. At that time, the Great Brahmā King said, "So be it, World-Honored One. World-Honored One."
"I wish to hear it with joy.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Brahma King, saying: "The appearance of all Buddhas in the world is for one great matter, and likewise for the sake of sentient beings.
All Buddhas are equal; they do not speak falsely. Through the skillful means of all Buddhas, [they act] in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings."
The Buddha’s wisdom from long ago is difficult to fathom or know. All Buddhas adorn their Dharma-body with the three mysteries; ultimately, it is difficult to fully comprehend.
Although you previously asked about the prediction of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), now [the Buddha] again plucks a flower and shows it to the assembly.
In this way, you [should understand that] all Buddhas truly and authentically manifest [this]; do not doubt it.
The bestowal of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) is the dharma of the Buddhas appearing in the world.
It is the great matter of the Buddhas’ secret intention (*saṃdhi*) and entrustment. Now, as for the secret intention of the Buddhas, it cannot be fathomed through words. Why is this?
This Dharma cannot be understood through the faculty of discursive thought; it is that which only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively realize.
You all should know this: that which is expressed in words is the Dharma adapted to the capacities of each assembly.
That which is not adapted to such capacities is inexpressible. Therefore, there are such matters as these.
You should know this: such a Dharma is neither of its own nature nor of another's nature.
Furthermore, although it is not separate from the natures of self and other, sentient beings realize and attain it through direct personal experience. All Buddhas are likewise so.
That I now entrust this Dharma to Kāśyapa is because Kāśyapa will attain Buddhahood after a long period; [I do so] to provide assistance for all Buddhas.
The Dharma manifests its form before the śrāvakas. Therefore, [the Buddha] at the Many Sons Stūpa divided his seat in half and invited [Mahākāśyapa] to sit, just as I now entrust [the Dharma] to you.

As it was with the Buddhas of the past, so it shall be with the Buddhas of the future; you should know this. Thus it is. (Note: The reconstructed text above attempts to restore the likely Sanskrit terminology and the flow of the Chinese Buddhist prose based on standard Mahāyāna sūtra conventions, such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* or similar texts concerning the transmission of the Dharma. The original fragment contains lacunae marked by □, which have been inferred according to context.)
[Blank] . The Brahma King [suddenly] realized the hidden meaning... Third:
At that time, the Great Brahma King, leaping for joy and filled with delight, said: "How rare, World-Honored One! Today I have understood..."
"How rare, World-Honored One! Today I have finally understood the Buddha's intent.
[He] immediately removed his flower crown from his head and offered it to the World-Honored One. [The Buddha] then said, "Since I first followed the World-Honored One..."
Regarding the Dharma assemblies that have been taught, they are without deficiency, just as I now contemplate them. Within these fifty years, how could there not have been some hidden intent?
Yet those in the assembly have taken the Buddha’s words at face value; thus, they remain blind to the Buddha’s true purpose.
For this reason, the World-Honored One has employed various modes of expression. The World-Honored One is of great compassion, and I have yet further [words] to say in this regard.
I have doubts regarding those who receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood:

do sentient beings who abide in the ultimate stage [of the path] possess even the slightest separate dharma outside of this [stage], such that there is something further to be cultivated or realized? World-Honored One, with great compassion, please diligently dispel our ignorance.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahma King, saying: "Excellent, excellent, O questioner! You all listen attentively and reflect upon this well.
That which is called 'esoteric intent' is, as previously stated, unfathomable.

To forcefully proclaim its essential nature is to say it is neither cause nor effect, neither cultivation nor realization, neither attained by oneself nor attained by another, and not attained spontaneously."
It is not attained through causes and conditions; it is attained through [the realization that] body and mind are ultimately empty, known by oneself.
It is attained through the inconceivable. [I recall that] in the past, at the Bodhi tree, I realized this principle;
therefore, it is said that only Buddhas and Buddhas exhaustively understand the Dharma. Furthermore, I recollect that in the distant past, there was a King of Emptiness.
When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, I first gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; and it was precisely regarding this principle that [the matter] began and ended.
At that time, the Brahma King said: "So be it, World-Honored One! So be it, World-Honored One! World-Honored One, such is the profound mystery."
The "intention" (*abhiprāya*) is the essential body of the mind of all *sūtras*. As for "all *sūtras*," it refers to those which speak of this [intention] as the *sūtra*.
All Bodhisattvas realize this and attain perfect enlightenment. Regarding what was previously called "bestowing the prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*):

These are the methods for manifesting transformation in accordance with the world. In reality, [the Buddha] realizes this and becomes a Buddha; therein lie the eight phases [of enlightenment], the attainment of the fruit, and the ritual of cultivation.
World-Honored One, the sun may become cold and the moon may become hot, but the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye never has two words.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is! It is as you have said. The Brahma King shall thus be able to protect and uphold it.
Chapter Four: The Attainment of the Path by the Bhikṣus.
At that time, the great assembly of a hundred trillion beings felt their bodies and minds move involuntarily; they could not remain settled in their seats.
With one voice, they praised the Brahmā King, saying: "Excellent, Brahmā King! For our sake, you have posed such a question. Excellent, Brahmā!"
The King is our guide. We are like those awakened from the intoxication of aged wine, or like those who have found a lamp in the darkness.
The minds of the three periods of time are extinguished; inner and outer sentiments are exhausted. There is not even a hair’s breadth of doubt in our intentions.
As for such a secret intention (*samdhā*), it is not as in the past, when things were sometimes concealed and not revealed, or when words were hidden and not uttered.
This refers to the profound and secret mind of all Buddhas. Such intentional meaning pervades the body and mouth yet cannot be spoken;

it pervades the ears of the body yet cannot be heard; it inclines the heart and entrails yet cannot be conceived. When the physical and mental realms are entirely within the mouth, one has already entered the Samādhi of Hearing-hearing, yet there is no speaking.
When the physical and mental realms are entirely within the ear, one has already entered [the Samādhi of Hearing-hearing].
To speak of the samādhi of speaking is itself without hearing; thus there is no speaking, and thus there is no hearing.
Now, to realize and establish the profound samādhi of all Buddhas—[O] Bhagavān, please listen and grant your permission.
That which is called "dust-to-dust" and "land-to-land" is the samādhi of intentional meaning. Birth and death, birth and death, is the samādhi of intentional meaning.
The non-abiding of every phenomenon is the samādhi of intentional meaning. Existence without intention is the samādhi of intentional meaning.
Suffering and pleasure, cause and effect, is the samādhi of intentional meaning. This is evil, this is [good], is the samādhi of intentional meaning. The three vehicles and the four fruits are...
The five obscurations are the samādhi of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). The twelve [links of dependent origination] are the samādhi of secret language (*saṃdhābhāṣa*).
The accumulation of the paths of the three vehicles is the samādhi of [the ultimate]. The six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones are the samādhi of intentional meaning.
Lust, anger, and ignorance are the samādhi of intentional meaning. The determinate and the indeterminate are the samādhi of secret [meaning].
Impermanence is easily changed; this is the samādhi of the [empty] square. The sound of wind, branches, and waves is the samādhi of the [empty] square mind.

Outflows and non-outflows are the samādhi of hidden intent. False views and right views are the samādhi of hidden intent. Breaking the precepts and upholding the precepts—[are likewise the samādhi of hidden intent].
Ignorance and clarity are the samādhi of intentional meaning. Pure and impure lands are the samādhi of intentional meaning.
Folly and wisdom are the samādhi of intentional meaning. Right and wrong are the samādhi of intentional meaning. Gain and loss are the samādhi of intentional meaning.
The behavior of birds and beasts is the samādhi of intentional meaning. The slaughter of those who practice the holy life is the samādhi of intentional meaning.

The practices of Māras and non-Buddhists are the samādhi of intentional meaning. Worldly violent conduct is the samādhi of intentional meaning. A distracted mind and distracted conduct [are likewise].
This samādhi of intentional meaning robs one of the practice of loving-kindness; this is the samādhi of intentional meaning. It causes blindness, deafness, and muteness;
this is the samādhi of intentional meaning. It brings about the calamity of death within the womb; this is the samādhi of intentional meaning. It awakens from the darkness of ignorance;

this is the samādhi of intentional meaning. It results in the exhaustion of sleep and the ripening of indolence; this is the samādhi of intentional meaning. It pertains to the obscurity of the intermediate state (antarābhava); this is the samādhi of intentional meaning. It is delusion... [and so forth].
Perceiving delusion and darkness is a samādhi of intentional meaning. Proclaiming and selling female beauty is a samādhi of intentional meaning.

Sporting with men and women is a samādhi of intentional meaning. Hunger, thirst, food, and drink are a samādhi of intentional meaning. The worldly affairs of rulers and ministers are a samādhi of intentional meaning.
Livelihood and productive enterprises are a samādhi of intentional meaning. Emerging from and entering meditative absorption are a samādhi of intentional meaning.
Obscurity; entering and emerging from the womb—these are samādhis of intentional meaning. Humiliation and honor, decline and prosperity—these are samādhis of intentional meaning.

The affliction of illness and the pressure of suffering—these are samādhis of intentional meaning. The Buddha’s activities in daily life—these are samādhis of intentional meaning. Raising a foot, sitting, and reclining.
The agitation and stilling of ignorance is the samādhi of intentional meaning. Curses, spells, and bewitchment are the samādhi of intentional meaning.
The affliction and confusion of chronic diseases are the samādhi of intentional meaning. The oppressive suffering of the hells is the samādhi of intentional meaning.
Disagreeable thoughts and agreeable thoughts are the samādhi of intentional meaning. The violation of the Dharma and the Vinaya is the samādhi of intentional meaning.
Bondage and liberation, suffering and pleasure—these are the samādhis of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). Diligence and indolence—[these are] the samādhis of...

[omitted]. ...The various great samādhis, the various great methods of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the various great divine mantras, the diverse laws of various kingdoms, the *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas, diverse laws and diverse arts, and the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as all forms of consciousness.
Evil causes and evil fruits; abusive speech and reviling; unwholesome dharmas and unwholesome conduct; wholesome dharmas and wholesome conduct;
the five heinous crimes and their contrary practices; the arts of the immortals and ascension; all speech; all movements; all diverse species;

the various forms and deluded consciousnesses within the various samādhis—as described above, and even down to the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of all phenomena as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All that possesses consciousness, the continuous flow of every thought-moment, and so forth, are subsumed within the Buddha’s intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
This extends to all teachings on secret mantras (*mantra*), all *sūtras*, and even all the established doctrines of Māras and non-Buddhists;
these are all merely different explanations and different designations for the intentional samādhi. World-Honored One, I pray only that You will bear witness to this.
As evidence: At that time, the Tathāgata praised them, saying, "Excellent, excellent! It is truly as you have said.

In the final age of the Dharma, you shall be able to protect and mindfully sustain sentient beings so that they do not lose or forget [the teachings], for those beings at the end of the kalpa possess meager wisdom and shallow understanding, and are unable to endure the great Dharma assemblies."
When the sentient beings with hair on their palms lacked faith, the bhikṣus of the assembly rejoiced so greatly that they forgot where they were sitting.
[End of section]. Chapter Five: All Kings Attaining Benefit.
At that time, the sixteen great kings and immeasurable minor kings each removed their precious robes and offered them to the World-Honored One.
Then, in one voice, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, today for the first time we have come to understand the intent of the Buddha.
That which the World-Honored One has entrusted as the Treasury of the True Dharma-Eye and the Subtle Mind is the secret intention of all Buddhas."
The Buddha’s Heart-Seal, the sūtra-teachings of all Buddhas, and the ultimate reality of the Dharma—these are truly beyond doubt.
Thus, the buddha-nature of all sentient beings is none other than our own original life-consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*);
how could anyone harbor any suspicion or attachment toward it? It is like the great sun-wheel shining at midday; both the wise and the foolish alike find nothing [to doubt] therein.

It is as the Blessed One has said regarding the reality of things: such a profound intention (*saṃdhi*) is not obtained through causes, nor obtained through effects, nor obtained through self or other, nor obtained through [the absence of] self-nature, nor obtained through conditions and so forth. It is truly obtained through the inconceivable. Therefore:
The World-Honored One held up a flower, seeking someone to take it up; Mahākāśyapa, possessing great wisdom, immediately realized the Buddha’s intent.

We, the World-Honored One’s disciples, recall that in the past, regarding those matters known only by the Buddha and the secret intentions of the Buddha—whatever the World-Honored One spoke—he would change his words and use different names, always earnestly and without fail adapting to the capacities of his listeners. How was it at that time?
"Are we foolish? World-Honored One, it is not that you have ever concealed or hidden anything, nor have you failed to provide testimony;
rather, it is we who are foolish. World-Honored One, you speak directly and fully to our faces.
As the Brahma King has said, all the sūtras are merely different chapters and different phrases of this very sūtra. All the suns and moons..."
The stars, mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, nations, lands, tiles, rubble, thorns, and so forth—all these are entirely exhausted and without exception;
such is the secret intention and insight [of this teaching]. This is the intended meaning.
"Therefore, for all the *sūtras*, this treasury of the true Dharma-eye serves as the authentic seal of the Buddha-dharma.
For all phenomena, this wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* serves as the seal of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), with nothing further remaining.
World-Honored One, is our understanding of the mind in this way in accord with the holy intent? The World-Honored One said, "So it is, so it is. You [have understood correctly]."
[The Buddhas] will equally protect and mindfully remember [this teaching], so that it shall not be lost or forgotten.
Chapter Six: On the Peaceful Stability of All Kingdoms.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, now the various great and small kings each lead the Buddha..."

How truly rare and marvelous! The World-Honored One has expounded for the sake of kings of the present and future the principles of protecting the state and upholding the Dharma, so that their lands may enjoy tranquility and their hearts may be at peace;
that they be free from the harm of malevolent spirits and the interference of Māra Pāpīyān;
that the Three Jewels may increase in brilliance and the common people may dwell in happiness; and that all things within each realm may be harmonious and orderly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahma King, saying: "Excellent, Brahma King! It is well that you have asked such questions for the sake of the kings of those lands.
Since you, Brahma King, act as a benefactor for humans and devas, I shall now speak.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well. He then said: "You kings, each of you should truly [reflect] and respond correctly."
The Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma: When the True Dharma is correctly established, it cannot be subverted by demons or outsiders.
When it is not subverted by demons or outsiders, the sun, moon, and stars do not lose their proper courses;
wind, rain, cold, and heat accord with the seasons; the five grains ripen in due time; the people of the realm live in peace and happiness; and the Three Jewels remain ever-present.
“You kings, this is the law for securing the state and nourishing the people; reflect upon it well.

You kings, if you do not uphold the True Dharma, and if the eye-treasury is not upright, then father and son will not be harmonious, kinsmen will be discordant, and the hundred officials and commoners will become rebellious in their hearts.”
When the hearts of the hundred clans rebel, disorder arises within the realm. When disorder arises within the realm, the king and his ministers lose their positions and the people disperse.
Under such conditions, calamities of wind, fire, and water gradually arise in succession.
Pestilential spirits enter households, and misfortunes spread abroad. [The rivers and streams of the mountains and lakes] present ill omens.
Regarding auspicious matters: [if] there are calamities or deaths among the noble or the lowly, and one possesses the names of the Three Jewels, there is no skillful means by which to rescue them.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the time of the Final Dharma (mappō), the world will be just like this. You kings, each returning to your respective lands, must not for a moment deviate from what I have taught;
this is called the Heart-Seal (hṛdayamudrā) for protecting the state. O Kings, after my parinirvāṇa, if there should be...
"Regarding those among the fourfold assembly who commit transgressions against my True Dharma, you kings must swiftly rectify them; do not say, 'This is beyond our knowledge.
After my parinirvāṇa, the Dharma is entrusted to you. O kings and ministers, if you can protect and uphold it, the intention of the Buddha will be at peace."
Then the kings said, "So be it, World-Honored One; we shall humbly obey your command.
The Seventh Chapter: The Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King rose, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, you have spoken of the time of my parinirvāṇa."
"O World-Honored One, how great is your great compassion! Why so soon will you abandon us gods and humans?
Why have you ceased your transformative work and entered parinirvāṇa? Is the World-Honored One not the compassionate father of all sentient beings within the three realms?

Upon whom shall the solitary, the orphaned, and the impoverished rely? O Compassionate Father of the World, why do you take no concern for them? The World-Honored One has already transcended [the world]..."
Regarding birth and death, as well as nirvāṇa and non-nirvāṇa, he was especially sovereign.
[During] kalpas of increase and decrease, down to half a kalpa, he [saved] sentient beings across [many] oceans and various lands;
thereafter, he entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahma King, saying: "Excellent, excellent! What you have said is so. Now, for your sake, I shall briefly explain the essential meaning of Nirvana.
The Brahma King replied: "I only wish to hear it. The Buddha told the Brahma King: "Listen attentively, listen attentively!
As for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, there is no such thing as the principle of Nirvana, nor is there the principle of not entering Nirvana; fundamentally, there is no extinction."
Furthermore, it is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished; it appears before the individual faculties of each being, yet it is not [seen by] the Buddhas.
Do not confuse this with the *nirvāṇa* of those heterodox teachers. Previously, when I was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa...
The Buddha appears before sentient beings due to their karmic resonance; when that resonance ceases, it is said that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa.

Whether it be a single word that encompasses the ten directions, or expressions such as "unspeakable" and "immeasurable," all are based upon the infinite nature and virtues,

That which is not a dharma of the two times has never been taught as the past or the future. That which is not a dharma of the evil destinies has never been taught as the dharma of transcendence.
That which is not a dharma of the three poisons has never been taught as the three liberations. That which is not possessed of mindfulness has never been...
Regarding what is called the characteristic of turmoil: it never speaks of dharmas that are slow or fast. Regarding what is not a mundane dharma of confusion:
it never speaks of departing from the five desires. Regarding what is not a dharma of the manifest or the secret:
it never speaks of the two truths. Regarding what is not a dharma of attainment: it never speaks of the dharma of non-attainment. Regarding what is not an obstructive dharma: it never...
That which does not speak of fused phenomena, nor of phenomena that are neither empty nor provisional, has never spoken of phenomena of the middle limit.
That which is not any name or characteristic has never spoken of what is either dharma or non-dharma. That which is not a worldly phenomenon has never spoken of Buddha-dharma.

One who does not preach the Dharma with the mouth has never expounded the principle of all speech; one who does not clarify the characteristics of ignorance and non-ignorance has never expounded the meaning of awakening and non-awakening;
one who does not feel weary of and seek to leave the mundane has never expounded upon pure and defiled lands.
That which is not affliction has never been called bodhi; that which does not involve the discernment of dharmas has never been called the suchness of dharmas;
that which is not a segmented dharma has never been called the dharma of the five aggregates; that which is not a fleeting dharma has never been called the diamond-body of the dharmakāya;
that which is not a concealed dharma has never been called the dharma of revelation; that which is not subject to transformation...
That which destroys phenomena has never spoken of manifest color or shape; that which is not the mark of aging and decay has never spoken of the physical basis for the fruits of suffering;
that which is neither great nor small phenomena has never spoken of the various capacities of sentient beings; and that which is not like an illusory phenomenon...

Thus, it has never been said that what was originally non-existent now exists; nor has it ever been said that it is a dharma beyond conceptualization. Nor has it ever been said that it is a dharma beyond deliberation;
nor has it ever been said that it is a dharma beyond fathomless calculation. Nor has it ever been said that it is a mundane dharma; nor has it ever been said that it is a supramundane dharma.
Nor has it ever been said that it is a dharma to be contemplated or reflected upon; nor has it ever been said that it is a dharma apart from all dharmas.

Regarding what is called the teaching of the Dharma: it has never been a teaching of skillful means; it is not a teaching of the absence of intrinsic nature, for it has never spoken of individual natures;
it is not a teaching of the various emptinesses such as internal and external emptiness, for it has never spoken of such matters as the coldness of water and the heat of fire;
it is not a teaching of the dharmas of the four great elements, for it has never spoken of the dharmas of aggregation and dispersion; it is not a teaching of the dharma of saṃsāra.
Thus, he never spoke of the Dharma of reaching the other shore; he never spoke of the principle of intrinsic nature regarding that which is not the Dharma of the six elements;

he never spoke of the Dharma of gain and loss regarding that which is not the Dharma of increase or decrease; he never spoke of the Dharma of opposition or compliance regarding that which is not the Dharma of the four inversions;
and he never spoke of the characteristics of emptiness regarding phenomena and principle regarding that which is not the Dharma of the non-self of the five aggregates. Not...
That which is not the dharma of identity or difference has never spoken of the principle of the Buddha-nature.

That which is not the Buddha of principle has never spoken of the meaning of the phenomenal Buddha-nature. That which is not a worldly phenomenon has never spoken of the *tathatā* (suchness) of dharmas.

That which is not a marvelous dharma has never spoken of rare and extraordinary dharmas. That which is not a dharma of contention has never spoken of dharmas beyond words. That which is not a dharma of calamity...

Regarding those who bring calamity, he has never spoken of the methods for reciting mantras. Regarding those whose characteristics are contrary to the Dharma, he has never spoken of principles that are not the Dharma.
Regarding those whose wisdom is inferior, he has never spoken of methods that transcend [the mundane]. Regarding those who are not the Three Jewels, he has never spoken of the Three Jewels.
Regarding those who have not abandoned all marks, he has never spoken of the Way of [attaining] the Way. It is neither identity nor separation.
As for "Dharma," I have never spoken of dharmas of phenomena and principle; as for "dharmas that do not resolve meaning," I have never spoken of fixed dharmas.
Brahmā King, listen attentively: as for one who is not an eight-aspect Buddha, I have never spoken of the Way at the Bodhi tree;

as for one who is not a dharma of provisional and ultimate reality, I have never spoken of the capacities of beings being great or small; as for one who is not an inferior dharma, I have never spoken of the most supreme.

Regarding the Dharma: that which is not a transcendent and supreme Dharma, he has never spoken of as being this rather than that; that which is not a Dharma pertaining to his own portion, he has never spoken of as belonging to another’s portion;
that which is not an easy Dharma, he has never spoken of as a matter of mere casual periphery;

that which is a Dharma difficult to understand and difficult to enter, he has never spoken of as a method for merely inhaling the breath and contemplating in silence; nor has he ever spoken of it as a Dharma for which a prediction of Buddhahood is bestowed.
That which does not speak of phenomena already arisen or yet to arise is not a phenomenon of time and season.
That which does not speak of distinct principles—being partial toward oneself and distant toward others—is not a phenomenon of principle.
That which is not all-encompassing in its characteristics is not a phenomenon of all characteristics; it does not speak of any characteristics, nor is it outside of all characteristics.

That which is not such a characteristic has never been spoken of as being outside of all things. That which is not such a nature has never been spoken of as being a fundamental or derivative phenomenon.

That which is not a fundamental or derivative phenomenon has never been spoken of as the ultimate phenomenon. That which is not the phenomenon of quiescence has never been spoken of as the phenomenon of supreme stillness.
That which is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon has never been spoken of as a non-manifest phenomenon. It is not a mass of merit.
As for the Dharma: it is that which has never spoken of the dharma of cultivating worldly virtues, nor of the dharma of mundane principles;
therefore, it can rectify erroneous principles. Because it is not a non-dharma, it can rectify what is incorrect. Because it is not [merely] the Buddha-dharma, one can know how to become a Buddha.

Because the Dharma is the fundamental source, it can subdue demons and externalists; because sentient beings have consciousness upon which to rely, it loves all living beings. Such is the Dharma of the mind.
The mind is it; such is the Dharma, and the body is its intimate witness. It cannot be grasped and there is nothing to be abandoned, for it transcends all categories of comparison.
It is not seen, heard, sensed, or known—this is the divine testimony of Brahmā. I have always testified to the Dharma as explained above;
this is the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, who share one voice and one tongue. This is the manifestation of the present Dharma.
Regarding the physical body: it may manifest as the form of a thousand-foot Śākyamuni, or it may manifest as a body one zhang and six chi in height;
this is the teaching of his Dharma-body. At times he speaks of the secret meaning known only between Buddhas; at times he speaks of teachings adapted to specific capacities;

at times he speaks of the Dharma of worldly-transcending original vows and prophecies; or there are sutras consisting solely of the Buddha’s single-line entrustment (note: these are not ordinary sutras); or he manifests the Dharma-body as having illness.
Furthermore, he demonstrates that the Dharma-body is free from illness, or he manifests the aspect of not entering parinirvāṇa.
Now, manifesting the marks and signs of a prince as the Dharma-body is the secret within secrets, the inconceivable within the inconceivable; it is a matter for Buddhas alone, not for bodhisattvas.
Brahmā, you should know that all these various teachings, reaching down to the future and final age, will appear throughout the world.
At the end of an eon, there are matters difficult to understand and difficult to speak of, such as events that startle the mind and eyes;

for instance, lotuses growing from fire, dust flying in water, the sun and moon losing their courses, or the stars portending calamities and anomalies. Or there are matters such as the governance of chaos, rise and fall, and the like.
If the laws of the house or the family lose their proper order, then [the consequences]—unlike the aforementioned [instances]—are immeasurable.
This is indeed the Dharma that was never before spoken.
At that time, Brahmā King arose, joined his palms, and said: "It is unprecedented!
Such an elucidation of the teaching is the most supreme discourse spoken by the True Buddhas. Truly, it causes the assembly to awaken all at once. We, the great...

Because of this, World-Honored One, I now speak of the essentials taught by the Tathāgata at one time according to the capacities of sentient beings.
"As I understand it, World-Honored One, I only pray that you will grant me leave. The World-Honored One said, "Excellent; do as your heart desires.

If one speaks of liberation, it is done through the language of liberation, without taking away or adding to anything. If one speaks of the dharma for severing delusions, it is done through the language of entering into principle, without taking away or adding to anything.
If one speaks of deviant or correct precepts, it is done through the language of correct or deviant precepts, without taking away or adding to anything.

If one speaks of the phenomena of conditioned flux, it is done through the language of [conditioned flux], without taking away or adding to anything. If one speaks of the phenomena of dependent origination, it is done through the language of reality...
One observes things as they are without taking away or adding to them. If one speaks of the meaning of a self, one does not take it away by speaking of non-self.
If one is attached to the teaching that phenomena possess intrinsic nature, one does not take it away by speaking of the absence of intrinsic nature.

If one speaks of the meaning of names and marks, one does not take it away by speaking of the mark of emptiness. If one speaks of the signless, one does not take it away by speaking of the presence of marks.

Thus, when speaking of non-action (*wuwei*), one neither gives nor takes away. If explaining the meaning of sentient beings, one does so through the words of the sages, likewise neither giving nor taking away.

All such speech that accords with the capacities of others is as described above; such words turn the mind so that it may be appropriately realized through spiritual resonance. This is what the World-Honored One has taught above.

It is spoken thus directly, without any duplicity of word or meaning. The World-Honored One... (Note: The original text contains lacunae indicated by □, which have been omitted from the translation as they do not contain recoverable content.)

Such a single word is inconceivable and unknowable; therefore, the meaning of the "Holding of the Flower" is known through this.
Is it not the case that the ultimate dharma and meaning of all Buddhas is likewise so? I pray you provide proof.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is. It is just as you have said. [It is] thus, thus. The Brahma King said, 'I shall now describe and proclaim this in brief.
Were it to be explained in detail, it could not be fully told even at the end of an eon.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Brahmā King, it is truly so. Brahmā King, it is truly so. You are able to protect and mindfully sustain the Dharma at the end of the kalpa.
Chapter Twenty-one: Subduing Māra.
At that time, Brahmā King again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does one subdue the Māra Pāpīyān? The Buddha said: "Excellent."
"Listen attentively! If the Brahma King wishes to subdue Māra, he must first subdue the mental Māras within you. The Brahma King asked, "World-Honored One, what is this 'mental Māra'?
The Buddha said, "The mental Māra is precisely the thought of wishing to subdue Māra. (Note: The thought of wishing to subdue Māra.
If one practices correct contemplation, that itself constitutes the subduing of Māra. (Note: 'Māra' means 'extensive. What is correct... [text fragment] ...?
If one perceives phenomena as being outside the mind, then the various māras will arise in competition. [If one seeks] outside the mind... [if one seeks] outside...
what is called [seeking outside] is the arising of the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*). If one seeks bodhi outside the mind, then the māra of bodhi arises.
To perceive saṃsāra as being outside the mind causes the māra of saṃsāra to arise. To seek the Buddha outside the mind causes the māra of the Buddha to appear.

To perceive the observance of precepts as being outside the mind causes the māra of the Vinaya to manifest. To perceive sentient beings as being outside the mind causes the māra of sentient beings to arise.

To cultivate meditative concentration outside the mind causes the māra of dhyāna to arise. To seek the Dharma outside the mind causes all manner of māras to compete to come forth. To perceive a nation as being outside the mind...

If the earth, mountains, and rivers were such that every place one touched became a realm of Māras, and if one perceived Māras outside of the mind, then the host of Māras would flourish even more than that of Brahmā.
Outside the mind there is no gain or loss; outside the mind there is no right or wrong; outside the mind there is no poverty or wealth; outside the mind there is no jealousy.
Therefore, one must subdue the Māra within the mind. If one does not understand this matter and seeks something else instead, one will fall into madness and confusion.
Perverse views arise; internal and external demonic hordes compete to emerge, acting as guides to evil destinies.
To forever sever such deeds that obstruct the work of a Buddha, [the practitioner’s] heart and mind become dazed and afflicted.
Thus, the four consciousnesses shift and fluctuate in this manner, stirred by the demons of the mind. If...
When the mental māra is subdued, all external māras will likewise submit and attend upon one’s left and right.
In this way, there is no longer seen any distinction between the realm of the Buddha and the realm of the māras. If they are not subdued, the Buddha and the māras stand as separate entities;
if they are subdued, the māras then accord with the True Dharma. Brahma King, you and your followers have thus subdued both extremes of the Buddha and the māras. Therefore, the mind—
This is the fundamental dharma-practice for all who cultivate [the Way]. If one does not descend [into this state], then all the sūtras are merely the teachings of external māras.
Even if one dons the dharma-robe and recites [the scriptures], it is entirely the work of māras and the deeds of māras (Note:

because the sublime mind of the True Eye is obscured). Brahmā, listen attentively: since I first resolved upon the Bodhicitta until the time I attained enlightenment at the Tree of Awakening, only then did I descend [into this state].
Thus it is. When the Brahmā King has subdued the mind-māra, then all dharmas and all sentient beings will entirely follow and return to my True Dharma.
The Buddha is the Dharma of non-duality. Such is the profound intent of the Brahmā King Tathāgata regarding the True Dharma.
The Brahmā King said: "So be it, World-Honored One. As for the 'mind-māra,' it is the mind of the two extremes. [End of fragment]

Chapter Twenty-Two: On Karmic Consciousness.
The Buddha addressed the Brahma King, saying: "Brahma King, you should know that there is the karmic consciousness of the non-duality of the sentient and the Buddha.

Previously, I did not expound upon it—that which is called 'Buddha-nature' with respect to sentient beings and 'Dharma-nature' with respect to insentient things; these two names [refer to the same reality]."
It appears different, yet it is the single reality. The Brahmā King said, “World-Honored One, I wish most earnestly to hear it. The Buddha said, “Brahmā King, listen attentively.
This is the ultimate discourse on the true reality of all Buddhas. You must contemplate it well and keep it in mind.
That which is called non-dual karmic consciousness is that which has come from the beginningless kalpas of the cyclic existence of all sentient beings.”

Furthermore, the characteristics of their transmigration are inexhaustible to describe; they are all produced by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Apart from this, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that exists independently.
As for the nature of this false conceptualization, if explained briefly, it does not exceed the two phenomena of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
To speak in terms of the internal and external, it is as follows... [as if] hating them.
Death loves birth; its distinctions of kin and stranger, greed and desire, and all that exists—good and evil, heterodox and orthodox, the five hindrances and ten fetters;

whether sorrow or joy, suffering or pleasure, wailing or laughter, what is appropriate or inappropriate, inverted views, heinous crimes, plunder, immeasurable afflictions, the oppressions of the three miserable realms, the griefs of various classes, and the fleeting [joys] of humans and devas...

Pleasure. The passionate attachment between men and women, the floating and sinking of consciousness, and the sudden arising of all sensory contacts with phenomena—whether seen or heard—are entirely the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*) and one's own deluded thoughts (*svavikalpa*).
Apart from these deluded thoughts of one’s own, there is no Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Brahma King, to perceive the Buddha-nature through the merging of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is confusion; to perceive the Buddha-nature through the separation of characteristics is likewise confusion.
These are two dharmas. The seeing of the Buddha-nature is difficult to fathom.

It is only by relying on one's own vision that all dharmas are seen as one's own—such as the lands, mountains, rivers, distances, nearness, length, shortness, squareness, roundness, blue, yellow, and so forth.

These are the self-nature and characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) of the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). The sun, moon, stars, and the bodily radiance of the celestial hosts are the light of the self-nature of the fundamental consciousness.
That all sentient beings possess no such light is the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) within the fundamental consciousness.
The various afflictions, suffering, pleasure, joy, love, and sorrow are the characteristics of the karma produced by the fundamental consciousness itself.
The "fetal death," "hundred years," "strong and weak," "old and sick," and so forth, are the signs of the contraction and expansion of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
The "honorable and base," "glory and disgrace," "poverty and wealth," and so forth, are the signs of the ascent and descent of karmic consciousness.

The "terror of the evil realms," "joyful seeking of the celestial realms," "longing for minor fruits," and "seeking minor liberation," and so forth, are the limited measures of karmic consciousness. There is no grasping and no abandoning; there is no...
Those who harbor hatred and attachment while expecting great fruits represent the vast magnitude of the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
Those who hold the sixty-two views or engage in heterodox practices such as those of the "chicken" or "dog" ascetics represent the perverted magnitude of the karmic consciousness.

To claim that one does not sever lust, anger, and ignorance, yet this is itself nirvana, represents the self-nature magnitude of the karmic consciousness. All forms of madness and all forms of frantic agitation represent the inconceivable [magnitude] of the karmic consciousness.

This discusses transformations. Whether it be wisdom or folly, whether it be an icchantika or one who commits the five heinous crimes, whether it be taking refuge in the Triple Gem or holding false views and false learning, whether it be laziness or indulgence in play, or gambling, hunting, or fishing—regarding all such auspicious and inauspicious matters alike, they are the inconceivable samādhi of karmic consciousness, manifesting as both exoteric and esoteric. This is like the Brahma-king’s kalpa-stone.
It may be exhausted. However, as for the functional capacity of the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), it is either indefinite or limited by years, months, days, and hours.
Yet, with respect to those within the category of sentient beings, it is infinite; all are the inconceivable transformations of the *karmic consciousness*.

If Brahmā were to speak directly of the self-substance of the *karmic consciousness*, then all the teachings of the Buddhas appearing in the world would be nothing but mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Brahmā...

O King, as for the appearance of the Buddhas in the world: although it is not like that which is led by the delusions of sentient beings—being of the same nature as the *karmic-consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) and the commonality of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*)—you should know that at the time of their appearing in the world, the Three Vehicles and the twelvefold division of the teachings are the correct knowledge and vision of *karmic-consciousness*.
Whether they speak of phenomena or speak of principle, they distinguish between the wise and the ignorant, and provide guidance for those of the three faculties.
"Et cetera" refers to the *siddhānta* (established tenet) of the intrinsic nature of the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
Or, "manifesting the taking of a womb, [the various] bodies, and so forth," refers to the inconceivable essence of the karma-consciousness. "The Buddhas are neither born nor do they arise;
they neither perish nor do they cease," refers to the phenomena of the inconceivable concealment and manifestation of the karma-consciousness. The Buddha constantly gives birth to these three.
The Samādhi of the King of Obscurity (*mewang samādhi*) is the inherent nature and virtue of the self-abiding karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).

The various provisional and ultimate skillful means of the Buddhas and the Three Vehicles, as well as the immeasurable precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, are but a mere speck of dust within the ocean-like source of the dharma-gates of the karma-consciousness.
The various Buddhas emit immeasurable rays of light to transform all sentient beings. Regarding this...
"Manifesting inconceivable realms within one's own land and other lands" refers to the inconceivable great function of the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*).
"The Buddha-body responding to beings with infinite forms" is that which responds to the true mark of the signless *karmic consciousness*.
The manifestations of the Buddhas appearing in the world include both the manifest and the secret, the provisional and the real, and the Great and the Small.

The speaker explains that because the self-nature of karmic consciousness possesses qualities of coarseness and subtlety, as well as shallowness and depth, there exists the inconceivable noble truth of the convergence of the provisional and the ultimate, which can be regulated and cannot be regulated.

This is taught through the four foundations of mindfulness, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; for within the self-nature of karmic consciousness, there are distinct characteristics.

Regarding the statement that "the wisdom of all Buddhas is one and identical to all-encompassing wisdom," this refers to the inconceivable, numinous awareness-wisdom of the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).

How is this proven? It is because within all ordinary beings and all those possessing consciousness, whether their cognition is at times correct wisdom or at times incorrect wisdom, it emerges from what they do not anticipate.
Therefore, it is called this "wisdom of non-nature" and also the "unobscured numen."
It is wisdom (*jñāna*). It is also called the unsurpassed wisdom of all Buddhas; it is also called the five wisdoms of the five Buddhas;
it is also called the wisdom by which the four Buddhas know; it is also called the wisdom that awakens to the knowledge of all things.

All that exists—every atom and every phenomenon, sentient and insentient beings, whether they are conscious or unconscious, with form or without form—all these are the characteristics of this numinous, awakened wisdom.
Furthermore, when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they neither allow [defilements] to enter from without nor allow [wisdom] to exit from within;
this is because of the unmanifest wisdom (*avijñapti-jñāna*) of the Mahāyāna arising from the *karmic-consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*). The Buddhas are that which all sentient beings act upon;

there is nothing they do not do and nothing they do not know, because they possess the inconceivable power of the wisdom of liberation arising from the *karmic-consciousness*. Moreover, the Buddhas...
The Buddha constantly expels external demons because he always teaches the nature of permanence.

All sentient beings possess inverted views of mind because they fail to know that the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) is devoid of self-nature. There is no separate dharma that can be taught as a principle.
After all Buddhas have completed their transformations, they enter extinction because the very substance of karmic consciousness is fundamentally quiescent. All that exists is non-sentient.
"Arising and ceasing in every thought-moment, not remaining for even a brief instant," refers to the fact that the intrinsic nature of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) is impermanent.
"The Buddhas possess profound and inconceivable merit" refers to the self-existent nature and virtue of the karmic consciousness itself.

If the Brahma King wishes to see the characteristics of the karmic consciousness, he must see the impermanent marks of sentient beings; if he wishes to see the marks and signs of the Buddhas, [he must likewise see their impermanence].
One should perceive the intrinsic nature of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). Brahmā may obstruct a single speck of dust or pluck a single hair, yet his feet can shake the entire Dharma-realm;
he may draw in other lands to become his own land, or shift this world to place it within another realm. He may grind Mount Sumeru into fine powder or scoop out the four great oceans;
he may relocate the hells to other lands, or asuras may block the light of the sun and moon, or swallow up the salt seas entirely.
Within a single mouth, there are wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. In a single step across the realms, one traverses the paths of the world.
Such are his miraculous powers: water flows from his upper body while fire issues from his lower body, and other such wonders; or he manifests a vast body that fills all of space.

Or manifesting a small body to enter the pores of a lotus fiber—such matters as these, with their thousand transformations and myriad changes, all without exception arise from the inconceivable realm of the *karmic consciousness*. The Dharma-realm of the Brahma King is boundless;
the distinctions among immeasurable Buddha-lands are entirely without exception the measure of the *karmic consciousness*. From the raindrops of the Brahma King’s Dharma-realm...

The number of grains of sand in the Ganges River, up to the number of atoms within the lands of the Dharma-realm, are all merely quantitative measures upon the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
Yet, all of these can be fully known within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). Such explanations as these are but one or two hairs from among the countless hairs on a cow’s body.
If one were to explain them extensively, they could not be exhausted even throughout an entire eon (*kalpa*). The Brahma King said: "So it is, World-Honored One."
“World-Honored One, World-Honored One! All sentient beings are born of deluded karma; they do not arise from the Buddhas.
The Buddhas are those who are equal to all that is unequaled. We wish to hear the meaning of non-duality; we pray that you will explain it to us with diligence within this assembly.
The Buddha said, “Excellent, Heavenly King! As for what is called ‘karmic consciousness,’ the Buddhas are of purple-gold [radiance]...”
The body of pure radiance is the very same as the body of afflictions and defilements possessed by sentient beings. Why is this? Because they are non-dual.
The intrinsic nature of my Dharma appears as impure though it is not, and appears as defiled though it is not; it is like water conforming to the shape of its vessel, whether curved or straight.
O Brahmā, one should not be surprised by these names and characteristics. As for what is called "karma," it is the Buddha-nature itself.

This refers to the essence and activity. "Consciousness" (śes pa) refers to the consciousness that is the very essence of Buddha-nature. Thus, Buddha-nature and karmic consciousness are one in nature but differ in name.
Although the Brahmā King is the manifested body of all Buddhas appearing in the world, his body differs from the transmigrating bodies of sentient beings;
they are merely different designations for the same single Buddha-nature. This is precisely what is called the "body of karmic consciousness. This is not something directed upward. This...
As for "not tending downward": therefore, all internal and external phenomena do not transcend the two dharmas of form and mind;
